market_context: United States/Canada; household no-hot-water troubleshooting across electric, gas, heat-pump and tankless water heaters.
title: Why Is There No Hot Water in My House?

seo.title: No Hot Water? What to Check First
seo.meta_description: Check whether one fixture or the whole house is affected, then review heater power, operating mode, valves and error codes and know when to stop.
seo.search_intent: Diagnose a complete loss of hot water and distinguish a single-fixture mixing problem from power, settings and water-heater faults.

excerpt: If you have no hot water, test several fixtures first. If only one fails, its cartridge or mixing valve may be the problem. If the whole house is cold, confirm the water heater has power or fuel, is in the correct operating mode and is not displaying an error code. If you smell gas, do not try to relight anything; leave the area and contact the gas utility or emergency service.
content_html:
No hot water makes it tempting to go straight to the water heater, but the first diagnostic tool is the faucets. One shower delivering cold water while the kitchen is hot can be a failed mixing cartridge. If the kitchen, bathroom and shower are all cold, then tracing the problem to the heater makes sense.

The important distinction is distribution versus heat generation.

Test more than one fixture before touching the heater

Run hot water at two or more locations. If one works and another does not, investigate the failing fixture. A. O. Smith notes that single-handle faucets and shower controls can malfunction in ways that make the heater seem broken.

If no fixture produces hot water, continue toward the water-heating system.

Identify the type of water heater

An electric storage tank, gas water heater, heat-pump water heater and tankless unit do not use the same controls or troubleshooting path. Find the model label, owner's manual and display.

Do not remove covers simply to explore before you know which technology you have and what the manufacturer permits an owner to access.

For an electric heater, check power first

Look at the dedicated breaker or disconnect. A tripped circuit can leave the tank completely cold.

If the breaker trips again, stop resetting it. Repeated tripping signals an electrical fault that needs diagnosis.

For gas equipment, safety comes before relighting

If you smell gas, do not operate switches, create a flame or work on the heater. Leave the area and follow your gas utility or local emergency instructions.

If there is no gas odor, limit your checks to the controls the manual assigns to the user: fuel shutoff status, operating mode, indicator lights or error codes. Many modern heaters use electronic ignition rather than a standing pilot.

Check operating mode and temperature setting

Some units can be left in Vacation, Away, Eco or another low-output mode. Smart or heat-pump models may also be changed through an app or remote control.

Many manufacturers use about 120°F / 49°C as a starting setpoint to balance useful hot water with scald risk. Raising the setpoint dramatically is not a fix for a heater that is failing to heat.

A high-limit reset should not become a weekly ritual

Some electric tanks have a high-temperature safety cutoff with a manufacturer-defined reset procedure. Follow only the model instructions and de-energize the unit where required.

If it trips again, the cause must be corrected. Repeated resetting is not a repair.

Tankless heaters need adequate flow and correct operating conditions

A tankless unit may not fire if flow is below its activation threshold, a filter is restricted, fuel or power is unavailable, or an error code is active. Rheem troubleshooting emphasizes power, valves and model-specific diagnostics.

Do not adjust gas pressure or open the gas train without appropriate training and instruments.

A closed service valve can mimic a failed heater

Confirm user-operated valves are in their correct positions. Plumbing work sometimes leaves a valve closed or only partly open.

Do not force corroded valves. A leaking hot-water connection should be repaired before the system is returned to normal use.

If water starts hot and then turns cold, that is a different problem

“No hot water at all” is different from “the shower runs cold after five minutes.” The second pattern points toward capacity, recovery rate, heating elements, sediment or simultaneous demand.

Treat that as insufficient hot-water capacity or recovery rather than complete heating failure.

Error codes are evidence

Write down the code before cycling power. Look it up in the manual and follow only the owner-level steps provided there.

Resetting first can erase a valuable clue and leave you with the same fault but less information.

When to call a professional

Schedule service if hot water does not return after basic power and setting checks, a breaker trips, the tank leaks, there is an electrical odor, gas ignition will not remain established, or the displayed code calls for service.

Start at the faucets and work backward: confirm it is a whole-house problem, identify the heater technology, then check only the power, modes and controls that are safe for an owner to inspect.

faq.question: Why is there no hot water at only one shower?
faq.answer: If other fixtures have hot water, the shower cartridge, mixing valve or control may be at fault rather than the water heater.

faq.question: What if the electric water-heater breaker is tripped?
faq.answer: You can check it according to the manual, but if it trips again do not keep resetting it; the electrical cause needs diagnosis.

faq.question: What temperature is a water heater usually set to?
faq.answer: Many manufacturers use about 120°F / 49°C as a starting point, subject to the unit manual and local requirements.

faq.question: What should I do if I smell gas near the water heater?
faq.answer: Do not relight the heater or operate switches. Leave the area and follow your gas utility or local emergency instructions.
